project.name: Not Arbitrary 06 — Circuit Diagrams Are a Museum

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Open any circuit diagram and you are looking at drawings. Not symbols somebody agreed on. Drawings of real objects, most of which stopped existing a century ago.
entries.direction: Warm, unhurried. The last clause is the hook - let it land without pushing it.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: In seventeen ninety nine, Alessandro Volta stacked discs of metal. Zinc, then copper, then cloth soaked in brine, and again, until he had a little tower of them.
entries.direction: Conversational, as if stacking them while speaking. A beat on each metal.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: He called it a pile, because that is what it was. Build it higher and you get more push, which is why we still measure that push in volts.
entries.direction: Reflective. Slight warmth on the last sentence.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Now draw that tower from the side, quickly, in pencil. Every disc flattens into a single line. The copper ones come out wider than the zinc.
entries.direction: Describing a hand at work. Unhurried. Land the final word 'zinc' crisply - do not swallow it.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: And there it is, on every circuit diagram ever drawn. Long line, short line. Copper, zinc. Count the pairs and you are counting Volta's discs.
entries.direction: Quiet satisfaction. Let the final sentence sit.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The next one takes no explaining at all. Wind a wire around your finger a few times. You have just made an inductor.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Press those loops flat onto the paper and they become bumps along a line. Nothing was abstracted away. The drawing simply is the object.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Resistance used to mean a long, thin wire. The longer the wire, the harder the current had to work, so the wire was folded back and forth to make it fit.
entries.direction: Descriptive, tracing the folding with the voice.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Draw that folded path flat on the page, and it is a zigzag. Every peak in it is one fold of the wire.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: And one of them never had to change at all. Two metal plates facing each other across a gap. Two centuries later, still two lines facing each other across a gap.
entries.direction: Deliberately flat and even, as if nothing interesting happened - because nothing did.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Here is the part worth stopping on. Almost none of those objects still exist.
entries.direction: Leaning in. The turn of the film. Slower.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The battery in your pocket is not a tower of discs. A modern resistor is carbon baked onto ceramic, with no wire in it anywhere.
entries.direction: Matter of fact, a little wondering.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The drawings outlived the things they drew. An engineer today sketches Volta's tower to mean a lithium cell, and everyone understands.
entries.direction: Warm. The quiet centre of the film. Articulate 'drawings' cleanly off the preceding 'The'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: A tower of discs. A coil of wire. A wire folded back on itself. Two plates facing each other across a gap.
entries.direction: Deliberate, one item at a time, like laying objects on a table.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: A circuit diagram is not notation. It is a museum, and everybody who draws one is still drawing the exhibits.
entries.direction: Warm close, slowing into the final line.
